summary:
Formosa stands under Argentina's national framework, which remains among the most permissive in the world on paper. Law 26.743, promulgated on 24 May 2012 after passing the Chamber of Deputies 167-17-7 and the Senate 55-0 with one abstention, allows a change of legal gender without surgery, hormone treatment or judicial approval; the United Nations described it as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region, and Argentina legalised marriage equality in 2010 as the first Latin American country to do so.

That framework has been narrowed by executive action. A decree of 5 February 2025 issued by the government of President Javier Milei restricts minors' access to gender-affirming surgery and hormone therapy, and a second decree governs the housing of transgender people in prisons. Legal experts interviewed by Agencia Presentes called the measure illegal and unconstitutional and signalled an intention to seek judicial intervention; the outcome of that challenge is not established in the sources.

Protection machinery at the federal level has been dismantled. The national anti-discrimination agency INADI was abolished, and trans people hired under the 1 percent Trans Labor Quota were dismissed.

Violence risk is set by the national picture. The Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity in 2025, a 62 percent rise year on year and the highest count in the observatory's ten years of operation, averaging one every 38 hours. Perpetrators were mostly security-force personnel and unknown assailants in public space; beatings were the main modality. Institutional violence rose from 17 cases in 2024 to 64 in 2025, and 32 percent of 2025 incidents occurred inside police stations or prisons. Forty-three percent of perpetrators were strangers to their victims.

Activists reported in April 2025 that police violence against trans and travesti sex workers had worsened since Milei took office and was worst outside Buenos Aires, in the more conservative interior provinces. Formosa is one of those interior provinces, and the province has no local reporting infrastructure capable of generating separate records, so the national figures are the only available measure of what a visitor faces.

The judicial response to gender-motivated killing is contested. In April 2025 Argentina's Supreme Court left standing the life sentence imposed on Gabriel Marino for the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán while rejecting attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance that an appeals court removed in 2020, so the gender-motivated aggravation is not currently applied in that line of cases.

Outright International's country overview, updated in March 2026, records negative assessments for same-sex relations, gender recognition and the registration of civil-society organisations, with an assessment of deterioration against the earlier statutory position.
tangentialFactors:
Trans activists in Buenos Aires interviewed in April 2025, including representatives of organisations named for Diana Sacayán, killed in 2015, and for the activist Lohana Berkins, said the Milei government's policies had made the community more vulnerable to violence and described the situation as chaotic and desperate. Agencia Presentes described the 2025 hate-crime total as an inflection point in violence against LGBTIQ+ people in Argentina, with trans women bearing a disproportionate share of the harm.

The gap between statute and enforcement is the defining feature of the current position: the statutory text on adult gender recognition is unchanged and remains among the most permissive globally, while the executive decrees, the abolition of INADI and the recorded rise in institutional violence all point the other way. A visitor therefore reads the statute and the enforcement record as separate signals.

Interior provinces are singled out by activists as the sites of the worst police violence against trans and travesti sex workers, which places Formosa within the higher-risk grouping rather than the capital's comparatively better-documented environment.
localsOnly:
Adult legal gender recognition under Law 26.743 remains available without surgery, hormone treatment or a court order; the February 2025 decree applies to minors only, restricting gender-affirming surgery and hormone therapy for adolescents.

Residents hired under the 1 percent Trans Labor Quota were dismissed, and the federal anti-discrimination agency INADI, which handled discrimination complaints, has been abolished, removing the principal national complaint route.

A second decree of February 2025 governs the housing of transgender people in prisons, a rule that applies to residents in custody rather than to visitors.

The province has no local hate-crime or LGBTIQ+ reporting body, so incidents inside Formosa are not counted separately and do not appear in the national observatory's provincial breakdown.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Formosa-specific data on hate crimes, police conduct or access to gender-affirming care appears in the sources; the province is assessed entirely through national figures and through activists' characterisation of the interior provinces as worse than the capital.

Whether the February 2025 decrees have been struck down, amended or upheld by the Argentine courts is unresolved in the sources, as is whether the signalled judicial challenge by legal experts was filed.

The sources do not state whether Formosa has its own provincial anti-discrimination statute or a provincial hate-crime provision, nor whether any provincial law modifies the national gender-identity procedure locally.

Outright International's March 2026 negative assessments are recorded at country level; their specific application to Formosa is not sourced.
